<challenge>
Design and build the strongest Gmail-inspired email application you can.

Recreate the clarity, information density, speed, and familiar workflows of a great modern inbox. Take the implementation as far as you can: choose the stack, scope, visual direction, data model, and technical limits that let you deliver the most convincing complete product.
</challenge>

<essential-outcomes>
The finished application must include:

- A polished, responsive mail shell with a recognizable inbox, navigation, toolbar, search, and account controls.
- A realistic seeded mailbox with varied senders, subjects, timestamps, labels, read states, attachments, threads, and message content.
- Functional mailbox navigation for at least Inbox, Starred, Sent, Drafts, and Trash.
- Working message selection, read/unread state, starring, archiving, deleting, and labeling.
- A usable search experience that filters or retrieves relevant mail.
- A message-reading view with a clear conversation hierarchy and useful actions.
- A compose experience with recipients, subject, body, draft behavior, send behavior, and a polished interaction model.
- Responsive behavior that remains coherent and usable on both desktop and mobile.
</essential-outcomes>

<product-depth>
Go beyond a static visual recreation. Interactions should update the interface consistently, preserve state where useful, and make the product feel alive. You may add keyboard shortcuts, bulk actions, category tabs, snoozing, scheduled mail, contact suggestions, rich composition, settings, themes, offline persistence, or any other details that strengthen the experience.

No external email account, authentication, paid service, or API key is required. A fully local product with excellent seeded data and convincing behavior is valid. Do not leave prominent controls as decorative placeholders when a meaningful local interaction can be implemented.
</product-depth>

<creative-freedom>
You have broad freedom over architecture, libraries, layout details, interaction design, copy, and visual polish. Use Gmail as the product reference, but make deliberate decisions and deliver a coherent application rather than a collection of disconnected screens.

Do not explain your design before building it. Make the product and engineering decisions yourself, implement the experience, test the important workflows, and refine it into the best result you can.
</creative-freedom>

<success-criteria>
The result should immediately read as a high-quality email client, reward exploration, and support a convincing end-to-end flow from finding a message to reading, organizing, composing, and sending mail. Visual fidelity matters, but functional depth, consistency, responsiveness, and product judgment matter just as much.
</success-criteria>

Work only inside the current working directory. Do not read, list, search, or edit files outside the current working directory. Treat it as a standalone project root.
During setup, configure your app and package scripts to use port 9231, then use that port for runtime verification.
Use pnpm exclusively if dependency installation or package scripts are needed. Do not use npm.
Set the browser title and the primary visible title to your model name, using only identity information already available to you. Add nothing else to either title.
Run the relevant checks yourself. Do not edit files outside the current working directory.

content.content:
OVERVIEW: Control Portly, the macOS dev server manager.

Portly keeps local dev servers running on fixed ports, restarts them when they
crash, and exposes everything through this CLI so an agent can drive it.

Every command starts Portly.app if it is not already running.

USAGE: portly <subcommand>

OPTIONS:
  --version               Show the version.
  -h, --help              Show help information.

SUBCOMMANDS:
  status, list, ls (default)
                          Show active servers and problems compactly.
  start                   Start a server, or a whole project.
  stop                    Stop a server, a project, or everything.
  restart                 Restart a server or a project.
  action                  Run a configured server action without restarting the
                          server.
  logs                    Print the recent output of a server.
  temp, temporary, run-temp
                          Run a short-lived process without creating a project.
  wait                    Wait for a temporary job and return its exit code.
  add-project             Register a project folder.
  add-server              Add a server to a project.
  update-server           Change an existing server's settings.
  memory-limit, ram-limit Show or configure automatic project restarts by
                          memory footprint.
  remove                  Remove a server or a project.
  take-over, adopt        Stop an external listener and relaunch the configured
                          server under Portly.
  port                    Show what is listening on a port.
  kill-port               Send SIGTERM to whatever holds a port.
  open                    Bring the Portly window to the front.
  quit                    Quit Portly, stopping every server.
  forever                 Keep Portly available across macOS logins.
  config                  Print the config file path and contents.

  See 'portly help <subcommand>' for detailed help.

content.content:
Dev Browser is a CLI for controlling local or external browsers with JavaScript scripts.
Scripts run in a sandboxed QuickJS runtime (not Node.js). Top-level `await` is
available, along with a preconnected `browser` global and standard `console` output.
A background daemon starts automatically when needed and manages browser instances,
named pages, and CDP connections.

SANDBOX ENVIRONMENT:
  Scripts execute inside a QuickJS WASM sandbox with no arbitrary access to the host system.
  This is NOT Node.js — the following are NOT available:
    - require() / import()     No module loading
    - process                  No process access
    - fs / path / os           No direct filesystem access
    - fetch / WebSocket        No direct network access
    - __dirname / __filename   No path globals

  Available globals:
    browser                    Pre-connected browser handle (see API below)
    console                    log, warn, error, info (routed to CLI output)
    setTimeout / clearTimeout  Basic timers
    saveScreenshot(buf, name)  Save a screenshot buffer (async, must be awaited)
    writeFile(name, data)      Write a file to temp dir (async, must be awaited)
    readFile(name)             Read a file from temp dir (async, must be awaited)

  Memory and CPU limits are enforced. Infinite loops will be interrupted.

Primary invocation styles:
  dev-browser <<'EOF'
    const page = await browser.getPage("main");
    await page.goto("https://example.com");
    console.log(await page.title());

content.text:
The mail app was already fully built, so I didn't add features. The one thing wrong was the dev server: Portly's `claude-opus-5-5-mail/web` on port 9231 was still serving an old copy that had been moved to `~/.Trash`. This folder didn't even have `node_modules`.

**What I did:**
- Ran `pnpm install`, then `pnpm test`, `pnpm typecheck` and `pnpm build` in one bounded Portly job. All passed: 30 of 30 tests across 2 files, no type errors, and a clean production build. The build did warn that the main JS file is large (620 kB); it still works.
- Pointed the Portly server at this folder and restarted it. The process on 9231 now runs from this `app` directory, and the page title it serves is "Claude Opus 5.5".

**Browser check (one quick headless run):**
- The browser tab title and the page's only main heading are both "Claude Opus 5.5".
- The inbox shows 28 conversations.
- Clicking the first one opens it (`#inbox/t-tomas-tent`).
- There were no console errors.

I didn't re-test compose, search, labels or the mobile layout in the browser this time. They're covered by the unit tests and were checked in the browser during the previous session.

Separately, the posthog and chatcut connections need you to sign in again (via `/mcp` or your claude.ai connector settings) before they can be used. Nothing in this task needed them.
